newsitem.title: UK: European patent law needs to be harmonised - ABPI.
newsitem.headline: European patent law needs to be harmonised - ABPI.

text.p: Europe's fledgling biotechnology companies risk falling further behind the industry in the U.S. unless the European Union agrees to harmonise patent law for all 15 member states, according to the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry.

"The U.S. has a broader and more favourable environment for patenting (biotechnology)," Nick Scott-Ram, head of research administration at British Biotechnology plc, told a news briefing. If harmonisation of patent law doesn't proceed it will send the "wrong political signal" to industry paving the way for further advances by companies in the U.S. and Asia, he added.

The European Parliament on July 14 will consider revisions to a draft biotechnology patent directive that would harmonise existing EU patent law as well as create an ethics committee to monitor trends in the industry.

Passage of the directive could come as early as October if reservations by some countries, notably Sweden, can be overcome, said Trevor Jones director general of the pharmaceutical association. A delay or outright failure of the legislation, however, would be a serious setback for industry, he added.

The U.S. biotechnology industry already accounted for 122 of the 150 genetic engineering patents for healthcare products issued in 1995, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industry Associations. Only 11 patents were registered from Europe, while Japan and other countries accounted for 17.

Jones said public concerns about the uses of genetic engineering had slowed down consideration of the directive. The revised legislation attempts to allay these concerns by making a clear distinction between what represents a genetic discovery and what represents a patentable invention.
"Patents don't allow the ownership of life," said Scott-Ram.
